claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by interface-mediated dislocation activation and accumulation.
Local lattice distortions and short-range order strongly influence dislocation activation and accumulation.
The FCC layers are softer than the BCC layers and therefore accommodate plastic deformation first.
Initial plastic deformation in the FCC layers produces dislocation pile-ups at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Interfacial dislocation arrays promote stress transfer from FCC layers to BCC layers.
The BCC layers are harder and more resistant to deformation associated with lattice distortion than the FCC layers.
Stress transfer into the BCC layers produces a progressive, layer-by-layer plastic response.
The starting coating has alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers, intact interfaces, and minimal pre-existing dislocation density.
Coherent or semi-coherent FCC/BCC interfaces mediate deformation by accumulating dislocations.
Compositional complexity and severe lattice distortion cause interfacial dislocation agglomerates to enhance local stress concentrations.
Increasing local stress concentrations eventually overcome higher barriers to slip in the BCC layers.
Under sustained loading, interfacial dislocation density will increase over time.
Plastic deformation will occur preferentially in the FCC layers before delayed plasticity develops in the BCC layers.
The multilayer will transition from uniformly elastic behavior to localized, interface-mediated plastic flow.
The proposed mechanism applies only while nanoscale layering remains intact and delamination does not occur.
The proposed mechanism applies in a loading regime that produces slow progressive deformation rather than catastrophic failure.
A lack of significant interfacial dislocation pile-up would falsify the proposed interface-mediated mechanism.
Uniform deformation of the FCC and BCC layers without FCC-to-BCC progression would falsify the proposed sequential deformation mechanism.
